The picks

Chosen for the recipient and use described, using published product information. We have not hands-on tested these products.

  1. 1. Pilots with a personal connection to the Cessna 172

    Cessna 172 Skyhawk model

    The best model is often the aircraft with a story behind it. This mahogany Skyhawk is especially thoughtful for someone who learned to fly a Cessna 172.

    Keep in mind
    A finished display model offers no building activity; choose a kit if assembling it is part of the appeal.
    Before you choose
    Confirm their aircraft type. A 172 and a 182 are different airplanes, even if they look similar.
    $249.00Listed 2026-10-20View at Pilot Mall↗
  2. 2. Students whose instructor recommends this format

    ASA pilot logbook

    An affordable way to mark the start of flight training. Pair it with a note about the journey ahead, rather than filling in any flight-record pages yourself.

    Keep in mind
    Another logbook can be redundant if they have a preferred paper book or digital system.
    Before you choose
    Check with their instructor first: they may already have a logbook or use a different format.
    $9.49Listed 2026-10-20View at Pilot Mall↗
  3. 3. Pilots who take paper notes

    SKILCRAFT B3 Aviator pen

    Black ink, red ink and a pencil in one everyday tool. An uncomplicated addition to a practical gift bundle, especially with a handwritten note.

    Keep in mind
    Its utility is limited for someone who keeps all notes digitally.
    Before you choose
    Check whether they prefer paper notes; an all-digital pilot may get less use from it.
    $24.50Listed 2026-10-20View at Pilot Mall↗
  4. 4. Pilots looking for a compact backpack-style flight bag

    Flight Gear Stealth Bag

    A flight bag is a gift they can use beyond the holidays. This compact backpack-style option is worth a look when their current setup is an overflowing ordinary bag.

    Keep in mind
    A compact flight bag may be too small for a pilot who carries a full day’s equipment.
    Before you choose
    Compare the listed dimensions with their headset, tablet and usual load before choosing.

Recognize the achievement before choosing equipment

A new qualification is personal. A short note recalling the work, persistence or memorable moments can make an ordinary gift meaningful. Ask what the pilot is excited about next: taking family flying, exploring somewhere new or continuing training. Those answers guide the gift better than assuming that passing a milestone means they need a more expensive headset or a bigger bag.

A keepsake of the training airplane

An aircraft model can mark the stage they have just completed. Confirm the exact airplane type before choosing a Cessna 172 model or another candidate. If you cannot find a close match, do not force the idea. A framed personal photo or a thoughtfully written card may tell the story more accurately than a model of the wrong airplane. Ask permission before using someone else’s photograph.

Useful basics should match their existing system

A new logbook or flight bag can be practical if the pilot wants one. Check their preferences first. Some people want to continue using an existing book rather than start a new volume at an arbitrary point. Others have equipment plans already. Let the pilot and instructor determine operational needs; your gift can support those plans without creating a parallel shopping list.

A contribution can be the most welcome option

A clearly stated contribution toward their chosen aviation purchase gives them flexibility. Explain whether the amount is fixed or whether you intend to cover a particular item. If using a merchant gift card, verify that the recipient shops there and understands the terms. The celebration is the important part; the gift does not have to demonstrate technical expertise.

Prices and availability can change. Check the exact model, delivered total and return terms with the seller. Our recommendations are researched editorial selections, not hands-on test results.
